By November the garden had ceased to argue and submitted itself, with varying grace, to reduction. The dahlias collapsed into blackened rags at the first severe frost, as though offended by a climate insufficiently appreciative of their theatrical intentions. The roses, cut back to humility, stood thorny and unpersuadable in the cold beds. Only the cabbages appeared morally improved by adversity.

Mrs. Finch, surveying them with approval from the scullery step, said, “There, now. A sensible vegetable. It asks nothing but weather and gives no trouble except to rabbits.”

He, who had never succeeded in admiring cabbages except abstractly, replied, “I feel there is in that praise an implied criticism of several people I know.”

“Then they should endeavor to be more nourishing.”

The days shortened not dramatically but by theft. Light went early from the lower rooms and lingered only in upper windows, where it seemed less to illuminate than to bid a formal farewell. Lamps were lit at tea and sometimes before. The business of drawing curtains acquired again its winter dignity, as if each evening the household must renegotiate its small treaty with night.

She had taken to reading after supper in the blue chair by the fire, one foot tucked beneath her in a posture Mrs. Finch considered incompatible with both upholstery and breeding. He wrote at the desk nearby with intervals of industry separated by longer intervals in which he looked at the page as though waiting for it to improve in judgment.

“Are you working,” she asked one evening without raising her eyes from the book, “or are you engaged in that masculine version of meditation which wears the disguise of employment?”

“I am composing.”

“You have written six words in twenty minutes.”

“Yes,” he said. “I am composing them very carefully.”

She turned a page.

“Do let me know when they are fit to meet society.”

He found, to his own mild surprise, that such remarks no longer disturbed his dignity because they had become part of its shelter. There is a stage of affection at which one no longer resents being accurately seen in small absurdities. Vanity protests; comfort overrules it.

Toward Advent there began among their acquaintance that annual agitation in which charity, piety, social competition, and bad weather combine to produce an unusual quantity of committee work. Lists were made. Parcels assembled. One heard repeatedly that something must be done, though what precisely and by whom remained capable of indefinite transfer.

She was persuaded onto a subcommittee devoted to seasonal relief among families too proud to request it and too conspicuous to overlook. This involved practical errands in mean streets, conversation with women whose gratitude was sharpened by humiliation, and the carrying home of facts not mentioned at evening gatherings where benevolence preferred broad categories.

“It is extraordinary,” she said one night, removing her hat with more emphasis than the action required, “how many people enjoy helping the poor so long as no poor person introduces detail.”

He looked up from the fire he was pretending to mend.

“Detail is always the tax upon virtue.”

“And upon opinion. Mrs. Calder told me this afternoon that if one gives blankets one encourages dependence. I should like to place her in an attic with broken panes and inquire whether independence remains quite so invigorating after midnight.”

He held out a hand for the hat; she surrendered it.

“Did you say so?”

“No. I said ‘Indeed?’ in a tone intended to suggest the gradual collapse of civilization.”

“A useful tone.”

“It serves in many branches of marriage as well.”

There were bazaars. There was a concert in aid of something insufficiently organized to survive the event. There were holly branches brought in damp from the lane and left in pails to recover their spirits. The house, though not festive by conviction, submitted itself to preparation. A pudding was discussed with foreboding and eventually attempted with success so qualified that Mrs. Finch described it as “honest, if heavy.”

“Heavy?” she said. “It could hardly be frivolous.”

“There are degrees, madam.”

He, tasting it under conditions of domestic diplomacy, declared it excellent.

“That,” said Mrs. Finch, “is because gentlemen mistake endurance for flavor.”

But he ate more than one helping, whether from gallantry or appetite no tribunal could confidently determine.

In the midst of these accumulating observances came a letter from his sister, written in that family tone which combines affection with faint archival grievance. She proposed a visit after Christmas, adding that she hoped country quiet had not rendered them entirely incapable of civilized company. He read the relevant passages aloud.

She listened, sorting ribbon at the table.

“She loves you,” she said.

“Yes.”

“And distrusts happiness in others on principle.”

“Yes.”

“That must be tiring.”

“It is hereditary.”

She smiled.

“Shall we ask her to come?”

He considered with the expression of a man invited to entertain a weather system.

“We shall ask her,” he said at last, “because refusing would create a longer inconvenience than enduring.”

“How domestically wise you have become.”

“I do not know that it is wisdom. It may merely be cowardice furnished with foresight.”

She rose to put away the ribbon.

“Those are often indistinguishable in family matters.”

December itself arrived with a kind of austere completeness. The fields were white on two successive mornings, though by noon the frost had retreated into the hedges, leaving the world damp, spare, and more exact than before. Sound carried farther. Smoke from chimneys rose straight when there was no wind and slanted decisively when there was. The church bell on Sunday seemed less an invitation than a fact.

One afternoon snow threatened and failed, which is among the more English forms of disappointment. The sky hung low and persuasive. Indoors the fire proved not merely agreeable but necessary, and necessity gave it a gravity absent in the decorative hearths of milder months.

She was mending at the table. He had gone out on some errand involving twine, a parcel, and the mistaken belief that shops in weather like this are less crowded because prudent people stay home. When he returned at dusk there was snow after all, fine and steady, whitening his coat and the brim of his hat.

“You look,” she said, “like a moral lesson against optimism.”

“I have been jostled by Christians purchasing candied peel.”

“Were you successful?”

He set down the parcel.

“I have peel, twine, and an enhanced understanding of human desperation.”

She took his gloves before he could mislay them near the fender.

“There is tea.”

“At that word,” he said, unwinding his scarf, “all social criticism dies.”

The snow continued into evening, softening the lane, quieting the world beyond the gate, and conferring on the smallest hedge the significance of design. They stood for some minutes at the window before the curtains were drawn.

“It always looks,” she said, “as if everything has been forgiven.”

He glanced sideways at her.

“Until tomorrow, when it becomes slush and reveals the moral instability of appearances.”

“You have no poetry.”

“On the contrary. I merely insist that poetry should survive daylight.”

Christmas was modest and therefore, by luck, happy. There were small gifts chosen with the pleased embarrassment that attends useful affection: a pair of gloves, a book she had mentioned once and forgotten, a writing case improved by compartments he would never use correctly, preserves from a neighbor, a knitted muffler of uncompromising color from an aunt whose love was measurable in wool.

Church in the morning, cold enough to make holiness seem physically exacting. Dinner at midday, larger than reason but smaller than custom elsewhere demanded. In the afternoon a walk, because one must justify the meal and because winter sunlight, when it appears at all, ought not to be insulted by refusal.

The fields were crisp underfoot. Bare branches etched the sky with a confidence foliage never has. They walked not quickly. Marriage had already taught them that companionship is not proved by maintaining the same pace at all times but by discovering, without dispute, one another’s natural one.

At the stile beyond the lower meadow she stopped.

“Listen.”

There was almost nothing to hear: only a rook far off, a dog answering from some invisible yard, the minute crystalline sound of thaw beginning where the sun reached.

“It is odd,” she said, “how full silence can be.”

He leaned on the stile beside her.

“Yes. People think quiet is what remains when life has gone elsewhere. Sometimes it is what life sounds like when it has no need to impress anyone.”

She looked over the field toward the smoke rising from their own chimney in the distance.

“I should like,” she said, “to keep this day.”

He answered, after a moment, “We do. Not whole, of course. Hardly any day survives intact. But something remains.”

“In memory?”

“In habit, perhaps. In the way we shall light fires, or speak at tea, or not need to explain why this field matters.”

She was quiet.

“That is less romantic than memory.”

“Yes,” he said. “Which is why it often lasts longer.”

His sister came three days later with two trunks, a lapdog of suspicious temper, and the settled expectation of finding the provinces both deficient and faintly comic. She was handsome in the family manner, which is to say as if assembled by an ancestor who had prized decisiveness over softness and passed down the preference like silver.

She embraced him dutifully, inspected her sister-in-law with cordial intelligence, and within an hour had criticized the guest-room curtains, the local butcher, and the national decline in standards of conversation.

Yet even she, under the persistent pressure of decent meals, dry sheets, and a household whose ease she could not successfully disturb, lost some stiffness by the second evening. She and his wife discovered a shared impatience with insincere compliments. The lapdog accepted the rug before the study fire as a constitutional right. Mrs. Finch referred to the visitor as “the colonel,” though no military service had ever occurred.

One night, after his sister had retired and the house recovered its natural breathing, he said, “You have borne this invasion with heroism.”

“She is not so terrible.”

“You are charitable.”

“No,” she said, smiling. “Only observant. She expected to find me either foolish or unhappy and is disappointed on both counts. It has made her almost friendly.”

“That in our family is the highest form of surrender.”

His sister left on New Year’s Eve, having pronounced the visit unexpectedly tolerable, which from her amounted to affection stripped of ornament. Snow threatened again and did not come. The year, having spent itself in ordinary expenditures, approached its close without theatrical weather.

There was no party. Neither of them desired one. They dined simply, sat late, and heard from afar at midnight a few sounds from the village—cheers indistinct in the cold, a gate banged unwisely, someone singing with more loyalty than pitch. He poured a little wine. She held the glass in both hands, warming it first.

“Well,” she said.

“Well,” he answered.

It seemed both enough and inadequate, which is perhaps the proper feeling at the edge of any year one has actually inhabited.

After a pause she said, “Do you remember asking me, long ago, whether I thought happiness would prove dull if it lasted?”

“I remember being young enough to ask superfluous questions.”

“I think I have an answer.”

He settled back, watching her.

“It is dull only to people who expect it to behave like excitement.”

He considered this.

“Yes.”

“What it is, instead—at least when it is real—is attentive. It keeps changing shape. One must notice it.”

He raised his glass slightly.

“To noticing, then.”

“To noticing.”

They drank.

The fire had burned low but not out. Beyond the curtains the dark year ended and the next began with no visible seam. Upstairs, water in the ewer held the room’s faint chill. In the pantry the preserves kept their various promises. On the hall table letters waited to be answered, and one bill to be regretted. The morning would require coal, breakfast, and an opinion about the weather. None of this diminished the hour. It completed it.

For there are lives that proceed by event and lives that proceed by accretion, and most fortunate marriages belong to the second sort. Nothing in them can be pointed to as the single making of all that follows. Instead there are repeated acts of return: to the same hearth, the same concerns, the same face altered slightly by season, fatigue, amusement, endurance. One learns the topography of another soul not by revelation alone but by daily travel.

Near one o’clock she rose to mend the fire before bed. He protested from his chair, then let her do it, because love is not always the refusal of service; sometimes it is permitting the familiar grace one has come to rely upon. The coals shifted, answered, and sent up a steadier glow.

“There,” she said.

“Yes,” he replied, though whether to the fire or to something larger there was no need to decide.

Later, when the lamps were extinguished and the house resumed that winter stillness which is never quite silence, the new year entered not like a guest but like weather: already present before anyone named it. And within the walls, among the settled furniture and sleeping books, the ordinary future waited with its patient hands—bringing more dust, more bread, more talk, more misunderstandings, more reconciliations, more mornings made from embers carefully kept.

Which is to say, life.

And, if they were fortunate, enough of it together to make even the smallest room seem, by use and memory, large.

January declared itself not by drama but by endurance. The ground, denied the decency of a lasting snow, remained hard in the mornings and indecisive by afternoon; ruts froze, thawed, and froze again with a kind of bureaucratic obstinacy. The hedges looked as if they had withdrawn from all unnecessary conversation. Indoors, however, life resumed its ordinary mechanisms with that briskness peculiar to households which cannot afford prolonged reflection upon festivity.

The holly was taken down. The more determined sprigs had shed berries onto the mantel and hall runner in a manner at once decorative and accusatory. The pudding, reduced to a final remnant nobody wished to finish and nobody quite dared discard, passed through several stages of reinterpretation before disappearing into a fate Mrs. Finch described only as “useful.”

“There,” she said, carrying away the last of the Christmas things. “Now we may be cold in a plain Christian manner.”

He, who had been standing on a chair in order to unfasten a length of ribbon from a picture hook and had thereby assumed the expression of a man performing state surgery, said, “Was our previous cold pagan?”

“Festive. Which is worse, because it expects gratitude.”

She was at the window, rolling up a paper star whose appearance in the front parlor had struck him all season as both cheerful and faintly implausible.

“I am sorry to see it go,” she said.

“It gave the room an air of trying to improve itself.”

“That is more than can be said of some visitors.”

He glanced down from the chair.

“My sister has left a permanent moral influence, I see.”

“Not permanent. But memorable in outline, like weather damage.”

The village, after its brief annual interval of invitation and noise, seemed to contract. One no longer met groups abroad except with purpose: a grocer’s boy carrying parcels with reddened hands, the rector bicycling with dangerous abstraction, a farmer in gaiters walking as if roads had been specifically made for his inconvenience. Even the churchyard looked more private. Winter strips a place of anecdote and leaves only fact.

He found, as he always did in such weeks, that work became easier and more difficult at once: easier because there were fewer interruptions, more difficult because one could no longer blame interruptions for not working. The page stared back at him with a bleak northern honesty.

“What you require,” she said, seeing him one morning in this mutual examination with his manuscript, “is either inspiration or breakfast.”

“I have had breakfast.”

“Then inspiration must be sent for.”

“It has been sent for repeatedly. It replies with courtesy that it is indisposed.”

She, sorting mending into categories more subtle than his mind admitted could exist, said, “Have you tried beginning badly on purpose? It often helps.”

He turned in his chair.

“That is your advice?”

“It is my observation. If one waits to do a thing well before doing it at all, one commonly ends by not doing it.”

“You speak with the confidence of long experience.”

“I was once seventeen,” she said. “One learns things.”

He considered this, then took up his pen with the expression of a man accepting medicine.

To begin badly, however, proved strangely effective. By noon he had covered several pages in a hand less elegant than energetic, and though much of it deserved later correction, at least it existed, which is the first triumph in all composition and many marriages.

It was in the second week of the month that the cat arrived.

Not theirs, of course. Nothing arrives more fully convinced of independence than a strange cat. It appeared one afternoon at the back door while rain tapped with mean persistence against the yard pump and the light had already failed into a premature gray. Mrs. Finch, opening to shake a cloth, found on the step a narrow black-and-white creature with one torn ear, a tail held at a diplomatic angle, and the fixed expression of one prepared to accept temporary asylum without the smallest concession of principle.

“Well,” said Mrs. Finch, looking down. “And who invited you?”

The cat blinked in weathered silence and walked past her into the scullery.

Its progress through the household was less an invasion than an administrative oversight no one corrected in time. It ate with concentration, slept by the kitchen range as if recovering from years of private disappointment, and by evening had established itself under the sofa in the study. The lapdog, had it still been present, would have regarded this as civilizational collapse. In its absence, only decorum suffered.

“She cannot stay,” said Mrs. Finch, who had already warmed milk.

He looked over the top of his book.

“Why not?”

“Because if one lets one cat stay, six relations appear in the spring.”

“That is true of some people also,” he said. “Yet society admits them.”

She, kneeling to look under the sofa, caught sight of two bright, unworried eyes.

“I think she has had kittens,” she said.

“How can you tell?”

“Because I possess sight, sir.”

This diagnosis lent the matter an urgency it had previously lacked. Over the next days inquiries were made, indirectly at first and then with increasing directness. No one claimed the animal. No one, indeed, seemed surprised by her existence, as if she had long inhabited the margins of local knowledge in the way of beings who belong nowhere respectable and therefore everywhere a little.

She attached herself, with excellent judgment, to his wife. Not by demonstrative affection—such creatures understand the danger of overcommitting—but by a steady habit of appearing where she was, whether in the morning room, the bedroom window-seat, or the pantry threshold. If spoken to, she listened without servility. If ignored, she remained as though pursuing her own adjacent line of thought.

“I respect her,” his wife said.

“Because she resembles you?”

“Because she does not waste emotion proving what she feels.”

He looked at the cat, who at that moment was washing one paw with an air of critical detachment.

“I begin to see what I have been competing with all this time.”

The cat, inevitably, was called nothing for several days, then half a dozen things, then finally Finch by Mrs. Finch in a mood of annoyance, whereupon the name remained because it displeased the recipient and satisfied everyone else.

January wore on. There came one bright week in which frost held fast and every surface outdoors appeared edged by a stricter intelligence. The pond in the lower field took a skin of ice thin as broken glass. Boys from the village were warned off it by authority and returned to it by instinct. Laundry, brought in from the line, came indoors rigid and with the extraordinary clean smell of weather itself.

On such mornings the sun, low but determined, entered the dining room with a clarity almost medicinal. Dust became visible and therefore, in Mrs. Finch’s theology, culpable. Chairs were moved. Carpets beaten. Drawers investigated and shown no mercy. He, seeking only a missing envelope, opened one bureau and found himself enlisted in the exhumation of several years’ domestic archaeology.

“What is this?” he asked, holding up a key of uncertain origin.

“If you do not know,” said his wife, who was seated on the floor amid a ring of sorted papers and looked alarmingly competent, “you may be sure it unlocks something we have not needed for five years and shall mislay again before Thursday.”

He turned it over.

“It has a melancholy face.”

“All spare keys do. They are the widows of utility.”

In the same drawer lay old letters tied with tape gone soft at the folds, invitations to dinners already forgotten by everyone who had eaten them, receipts preserving with solemn futility the price of things no longer owned, and one small notebook containing lists in her hand: candles, tea, blacking, starch, eggs. Such fragments ought by rights to be dull. Yet he found in them the curious pathos of all ordinary records, which is that they testify not to dramatic days but to uninterrupted ones.

She took the notebook from him.

“Do not become sentimental over housekeeping,” she said. “It leads nowhere useful.”

“On the contrary. Here is the proof that we existed in March.”

“I remember March.”

“Yes, but the tea does not.”

That month, as if in rebuke to winter’s severity, invitations began again to circulate. There was to be a dinner at the vicarage, a lecture in the assembly rooms on Italian painting delivered by a gentleman who had seen very little Italy but a great deal of lantern-slide equipment, and a gathering at the Calders’, which promised cards, overcooked food, and opinions presented under the name of conversation.

“Must we go?” he asked, with the hopelessness of a man who already knows the answer socially expected.

“Not to all,” she said. “We may choose our sufferings.”

“What a blessing civilization is.”

“To the vicarage, certainly. Mrs. Beddow gave us quince jelly when I had the cold. One cannot refuse jelly.”

“And the lecture?”

She considered.

“I confess some curiosity. I wish to hear whether beauty, in his account, improves under projection.”

The Calders were postponed on grounds not entirely fictional involving a chill, a draft, and prudence. This was received by Mrs. Calder with a note so laden with concern that one could almost hear it hoping to be contradicted. It was not.

The lecture proved, as lectures often do, to have been prepared for a larger intellect than the lecturer possessed and a smaller one than the audience pretended to own. There were Madonnas enlarged to an accusing scale, saints in improbable postures, and repeated references to “the spirit of the Renaissance” as though it had recently sent regrets. Yet the evening was not wasted. Shared mediocrity, when publicly endured, has social uses.

Walking home under a enamelled sky pricked with cold stars, her gloved hand through his arm, she said, “I liked the little man in the third row who fell asleep during Titian and woke up nodding sternly at Raphael.”

“He was taking a broad, ecumenical view of art.”

“No, he was preserving honesty. It is one of the few defenses against culture.”

The lane shone faintly where frost had found the puddles before them. There are walks in summer that flatter the senses more abundantly, but winter companionship has its own exact rewards. One feels, in the cold, the simplicity of being there at all.

By February the first deception of spring appeared: not warmth, certainly not softness, but an alteration in light so slight one mistrusted it at once. Afternoon no longer ended in collapse. There came from the borders, where weeks before nothing had seemed capable of decision, the green beaks of bulbs pushing up through earth with scandalous confidence. Rooks argued in the elms as if reclaiming old legal rights.

Mrs. Finch, encountering the first snowdrops by the wall, said only, “Too early,” in a tone that implied personal vanity on their part. Yet she put them in a small glass on the breakfast table, where they stood with the fragile firmness of things that know exactly how much winter remains and rise anyway.

His wife touched one blossom with a finger.

“It is absurd,” she said. “How can anything look so innocent and be so determined?”

“They have the advantage of not attending committees.”

She laughed, and Finch the cat, now entirely naturalized and awaiting no one’s permission for anything, leapt onto the window-seat to inspect the morning.

So the house moved forward, not into revelation but into continuation: fires still needed in the evening, boots still muddy at the door, letters still arriving with requests, opinions, and the occasional check; meals planned, linens aired, books begun and abandoned, work attempted, postponed, resumed. Outside, the season turned by increments too modest for rhetoric yet sufficient, by accumulation, to alter everything.

And if there are grander subjects than such days, there are not many truer ones. For much of human contentment is made not from climax but from recurrence slightly redeemed: the same rooms receiving a different light, the same voices finding a fresh turn, the same affections proving, under repetition, not exhausted but confirmed.

Soon enough there would be wind in a milder quarter, and mud in earnest, and the annual argument with weeds, and some new anxiety brought in with the post and laid beside the marmalade. There would be guests one was glad to see and guests one survived by private wit. There would be illness somewhere, and recoveries, and expenses, and perhaps news from afar that altered a family’s horizon by a degree or two. Nothing—nothing worth trusting, at least—would remain simple for long.

But this did not trouble the morning. The snowdrops stood. The kettle sounded from below. In the grate the coal settled inward with a soft red sigh. She reached for the tea. He reached for the letters. The cat shut her eyes in a strip of pale sun as though blessing the arrangement without wishing to be quoted.

A small life, viewed from nowhere. Which is perhaps another way of saying: a life sufficiently inhabited to need no witness.

March, when it came, did so with wet cuffs and a plausible face. It was forever on the point of clearing and forever reconsidering. The road through the village acquired that complicated surface which is neither mud nor stone but a treaty between the two, and every cartwheel signed it differently. In the garden the earth gave off, after rain, the dark mineral smell that seems less a scent than the memory of labor.

Nothing in the house altered quickly, yet everything had shifted a little from its winter station. The dining room fire was allowed to die on certain afternoons if the light proved sufficient compensation. Windows, opened a cautious inch at first, admitted air with a raw edge and an insinuating energy, as though the outdoors had been waiting some time to resume partial possession. One began to hear things again: a pail set down in the yard, distant hammering, a gate objecting to use, rooks conducting litigation in the upper branches.

Mrs. Finch declared war upon corners.

“This is not cleaning,” he said, observing her with a broom of unmistakably punitive intent. “It is a campaign.”

“Yes,” she replied, not pausing. “Winter accumulates. Spring must deny it.”

“On political grounds?”

“On shelf tops, for a beginning.”

He withdrew from the line of action with what dignity remained available to a man carrying two books and a coal scuttle for no visible reason. Finch the cat, seated midway on the stairs, watched the proceedings with the narrowed eyes of one who had lived among upheavals before and reserved judgment until feeding time.

His work, which had gone forward in dutiful starts and pauses through January and February, now acquired a stranger rhythm. Ideas came while he was occupied with other things and deserted him when formally invited. A sentence appeared entire while shaving; a paragraph presented itself between the second and third potatoes at supper; an objection of real intelligence occurred only after he had copied out a page in fair hand. He grew suspicious of desks and respectful of corridors.

“You look hunted,” his wife said one afternoon, finding him in the hall with a pencil behind one ear and another in his hand.

“I was writing in the study,” he said, “until I understood that what I meant belonged in the chapter before last.”

“That is not being hunted. It is being corrected.”

“By whom?”

She considered.

“By the thing itself, perhaps. Works are often more opinionated than the people producing them.”

This struck him as unjust but not inaccurate. He returned upstairs and crossed out three pages with the grim relief of a man paying a necessary bill.

The village meanwhile resumed its annual habit of pretending not to have watched the winter and now speaking of weather as if newly introduced to it. At the butcher’s there was debate on lambs. At the post office there was skepticism regarding bulbs. The rector, who had survived two months of cycling over half-frozen roads with a serenity bordering on the miraculous, was heard to say that spring was “upon us” on a morning when sleet was falling at a diagonal.

Mrs. Beddow from the vicarage sent word that the early crocuses in her south border had shown themselves, and added, with the tact of the happily fortunate, that she hoped others were “having the same encouragement.” Mrs. Finch, reading this, made a sound too compressed to classify.

“Encouragement?” he said.

“If flowers begin to require morale,” said Mrs. Finch, “we are finished as a species.”

Yet on the following day she walked the garden paths with a basket over one arm and a gaze so alert that even the bare stems seemed to feel reviewed. Dead growth was cut back. Last year’s leaves, which had settled over the beds in a tired conspiracy, were lifted away. Here and there something living was discovered beneath what had appeared merely neglect.

“It is always irritating,” she said, “how much nature can look like untidiness in its intermediate stages.”

“That is because nature has no drawers.”

“Nor standards.”

“On the contrary. Its standards are tyrannical. It simply does not explain them.”

Along the wall the snowdrops had multiplied into a small white parliament, each inclined as if privately dissenting from the others. The daffodils were further behind, but their leaves had the unmistakable air of plans already laid. In the kitchen garden the first rows were being spoken of, though not yet planted; at this season discussion is half the agriculture of England.

There arrived also, with the year’s turning, those domestic injuries spring does to memory. One finds in a closet the lighter coat one had entirely forgotten. One opens a box and discovers seeds purchased with optimism old enough now to seem almost historical. A hat, missing since November, appears under circumstances so obvious as to insult the intellect. He found, in the pocket of an overcoat, a theatre program from the previous autumn and spent several moments trying to recover not the performance but the exact quality of the evening around it: whether there had been rain, whether she had worn the dark blue, whether they had quarreled lightly on the way home over an actor who mistook gesture for feeling.

“Do you remember this?” he asked.

She glanced at the folded program.

“No. Should I?”

“Apparently not.”

“Then perhaps it was unimportant.”

He thought this over.

“Or perfectly happy,” he said.

“Yes,” she replied. “Those are the first things one forgets. Distress has vanity. Happiness lives on housekeeping terms and leaves poor records.”

This seemed true enough to disturb him slightly.

One morning there was a noise in the yard unlike the usual traffic of buckets, steps, and hens: a thin, outraged sound repeated with conviction. Finch, who had been for some weeks of a breadth and composure inconsistent with her original figure, had disappeared at dawn and was now discovered in the coal shed, having arranged matters according to instincts older than domestic consent.

Mrs. Finch emerged with her sleeves turned up and an expression permitting no foolishness.

“Well?” he said from a tactful distance.

“Well,” she returned, “your stray philosopher has become a matron.”

“How many?”

Mrs. Finch gave him the look reserved for those who ask for numbers when the case is clearly moral as well as arithmetic.

“Enough.”

Enough proved to be four: one black, one mostly white, one improbably patched, and one so undecided in color that it looked as if begun in haste and finished by committee. They were blind, absurd, and entirely occupied with purposes too urgent to be pretty.

His wife, who had knelt longer than was comfortable on the coal-shed boards to inspect them, came back with straw on her skirt and something gentler than amusement in her face.

“Are they dreadful?” he asked.

“Extremely,” she said. “And perfect.”

For several days the household reorganized itself around this event while denying any such thing. Mrs. Finch complained of saucers. His wife cut up an old flannel garment without visible regret, which was how one knew the situation serious. He was permitted, with directives, to improve the box and then discouraged from improving it further.

“You are making it into a residence,” said his wife.

“They are residents.”

“They are kittens.”

“All the more reason not to begin life damp.”

“That,” she said, “is the sentence by which civilization justifies itself.”

The news spread in the village with a speed generally reserved for scandal or fire. Children developed errands near the back gate. Mrs. Beddow sent a note containing practical advice and, less usefully, three exclamation marks. Even the postman, a man not habitually betrayed into warmth, asked after “the family” with enough particularity to show he meant the new branch of it.

Spring by then had ceased to be theoretical. There were mornings when the air still bit, but the bite came from a creature losing authority. Grass altered almost overnight from endurance to intention. The hedges, which all winter had seemed made of nothing but thorn and refusal, acquired along their lengths a haze so fine one first mistook it for weather. Then suddenly every tree had entered negotiations with leaf.

They dined one evening with the windows shut and heard, unmistakably, the first sustained birdsong after supper.

“There,” she said quietly.

“Yes.”

Neither of them identified it. Names are often the least important part of recognition.

Later, standing a moment before bed with the curtain drawn back, he saw the garden under a sky not yet dark enough for stars in numbers: the paths pale, the beds obscure, the wall a deeper block against the dimness. Somewhere in that softened blackness some small incessant creature was moving among roots and early growth, occupied with an existence complete in itself and unintelligible except by patience. It seemed to him then that much of life was like this: not hidden, exactly, but proceeding beyond summary.

In the days that followed there would be rain enough to flatten the first tulips, and sunshine enough to persuade one falsely that coats were a superstition. There would be discussion of where to set the beans. There would be a letter from his sister, affectionate and exhausting. There would be one of the kittens, the patched one, proving early an aptitude for climbing curtains, and another attaching itself to Mrs. Finch with a perseverance she described as persecution and everybody else as justice. His manuscript would advance, recul, recover, and at last become long enough to alarm him. Bills would arrive with spring punctuality. Somebody would catch cold from optimism.

None of this prevented the day from being itself.

At breakfast, the window stood open an inch wider than before. A bee, having mistaken opportunity for invitation, investigated the room and then corrected itself. The toast was less warm than ideal because conversation had wandered. On the sill, Finch sat with the grave self-possession of motherhood accepted but not sentimentalized. In the yard, water dripped from somewhere unseen with a rhythm almost persuasive enough to count as peace.

His wife folded a letter and set it by her plate.

“Bad news?” he asked.

“No. Merely news.”

“Which is often worse.”

She smiled.

“Then let us postpone its full importance until after tea.”

This, too, was a kind of wisdom: not denial, but allocation. One cannot meet the whole world at once; one meets the morning first.

He reached for the marmalade. She reached to rescue the butter from the edge of the sun. From below stairs came Mrs. Finch’s voice, proving by its tone that some ordinary catastrophe had occurred and was survivable only by immediate intervention. The kittens, unseen, had begun to squeak in the coal shed with that astonishing confidence by which the helpless summon service from the merely tired.

And the house, imperfect, inhabited, a little worn at the thresholds and entirely committed to continuation, received another day.

By April the house had surrendered the last respectable arguments for winter and taken up, instead, the more various inconveniences of light. Dust, which in January had possessed the decency to remain theoretical, now declared itself on polished surfaces by ten o’clock and on dark ones before one had turned away. The clocks seemed less trustworthy. Meals drifted. The temptation to begin things for which there was not time increased with the evening.

Mrs. Finch maintained that this was not a season but a test.

“Of what?” he asked.

“Character. Also hinges.”

The back door, in support of this view, had developed a swollen reluctance and required persuasion incompatible with gentleness. Every entrance to the garden now involved a brief scene of negotiation, ending either in triumph or language not wholly suitable to domestic peace. He proposed planing the edge. Mrs. Finch proposed first trying soap. His wife proposed that no one propose anything until luncheon.

The kittens opened their eyes upon the world with an expression not of wonder but complaint. It appeared to surprise them that existence should be so abrupt and so insufficiently upholstered. The black one was first to discover the principle of forward movement and immediately employed it in reaching places from which return seemed a personal insult. The white one slept with a seriousness suggesting a future in the church. The patched one, as foretold, climbed whatever admitted of claws and once hung from the fringe of a chair cover with the fierce astonishment of a creature betrayed by success. The fourth, the one finished by committee, displayed from the outset a social ambition out of all proportion to its size.

“It has chosen,” said his wife, as the little mottled animal installed itself in the curve behind her knee the moment she sat down.

“Against your expressed wishes.”

“Yes. All attachments begin in disobedience.”

He looked up from his papers.

“That cannot possibly be true.”

“No? Then the agreeable ones merely flatter us into forgetting it.”

Meanwhile his manuscript, which had lately shown signs of becoming manageable, resumed a behavior nearer weather than work. There were fine mornings when he arranged his notes, sharpened pencils, set out clean sheets, and felt at once the fraudulence of every settled intention. Then, on afternoons apparently spoiled by errands, interruptions, and the need to carry a basket of seedlings from one end of the garden to the other, he would return with mud on one cuff and produce two pages that seemed to have been waiting for him in a more intelligent state than his own.

He began, in consequence, to distrust not only desks but plans.

“The trouble,” he said, “is that the book improves its judgment precisely when I lose mine.”

His wife, thinning out seedlings with an air of legislating mercy, said, “Then one of you remains competent. I do not see the difficulty.”

“It is humiliating.”

“That also may be useful. Plants dislike being talked over.”

“I was referring to prose.”

“Yes. But the principle extends.”

From the village came that increase of activity which in the country is never admitted to be bustle and therefore becomes, by some social alchemy, much more exhausting. Barrows appeared. Gates stood open. Men looked at fields with intent that had moved beyond mere endurance and toward opinion. There were carts carrying things one recognized and things one did not. The blacksmith’s yard rang brighter. Someone was forever mending netting. Someone else was forever borrowing twine. At the post office, gardening had replaced weather as the principal subject on which all were authoritative and no two agreed.

Mrs. Beddow reported, with renewed encouragement, that her pears had “set beautifully,” a phrase that caused Mrs. Finch to pause in the act of kneading and repeat it under her breath as if testing a foreign doctrine.

“Fruit does not set beautifully,” she said. “It either comes or it sulks.”

The rector, meeting him by chance near the green, inquired after the kittens with greater warmth than after his own parish accounts, and was persuaded, two days later, to inspect them in person. He stood in the coal shed with his hat in his hand and a smile unbecomingly tender for a man discussing church roofing only an hour before.

“Extraordinary,” he said softly.

“What is?”

“That anything so unfinished should insist so completely on being alive.”

The remark, though not novel, stayed with him. There are thoughts one has had in private which become real only after being spoken by somebody else in a yard that smells of damp brick and coal dust.

Toward the end of the month there came three days of deceptive warmth, all blue promises and reckless conclusions. Coats were left unbuttoned. Rugs appeared over sills. Mrs. Finch condemned this at once as showing off. The garden, however, took the bait. Tulips rose with theatrical assurance. The apple tree near the wall came into a foam of blossom so sudden and so candid that even he, who regarded floral abundance as one of nature’s more obvious achievements, stopped on the path to look at it properly.

His wife joined him.

“It will be spoiled,” she said.

“By what?”

“Wind, rain, time, confidence, almost anything. That is not the point.”

“No,” he said.

They stood a little longer than the sight required.

Then, because prophecy enjoys immediate vindication, the weather broke. Rain arrived with quantity rather than drama and stayed long enough to flatten early hopes without quite washing them away. The paths resumed their treaty with boots. Indoors, damp crept into hems and temper alike. The kittens smelled faintly of old flannel and milk. The patched one succeeded at last in scaling a curtain and had to be detached while maintaining the conviction that it had improved the room.

“Nothing so small,” said his wife, restoring it to the floor, “should possess such complete confidence.”

“It may be the secret of success.”

“It is certainly the secret of breakage.”

A letter came from his sister precisely as predicted: four pages, close-written, affectionate, full of concern arranged in paragraphs too orderly to be calmed. She described a cough, a neighbor, a servant problem, the price of things, and a state of nerves which, from long acquaintance, he recognized as vigorously maintained. He read it once with brotherly attention and once with literary horror.

“Well?” said his wife.

“She is well enough to describe being unwell in detail.”

“Then she is recovering.”

“I am invited to take her seriously.”

“You are her brother. It is one of the services included.”

He sighed and folded the letter.

“I never know,” he said, “how much sympathy to send.”

“All of it,” she replied. “Belief in installments.”

This answer served as many of hers did: by sounding simple until one attempted to improve upon it.

The beans were eventually set where, after discussion prolonged enough to count as local government, they had always been going to be set. The peas followed. Nets were argued over, adjusted, admired, and later found insufficient by exactly the creatures Mrs. Finch had named in advance. A robin developed an interest in fresh digging so intimate that one felt either honored or supervised. In the evenings, if there had been sun, the whole garden held that brief stored warmth from which smells rise more richly: box, damp earth, bruised green things, smoke from somewhere beyond the hedge, and occasionally the sweet, almost clean scent of newly split wood.

His work lengthened. That was at once its satisfaction and its accusation. A short manuscript may still be thought accidental; a long one begins to look like intention. He placed the pages in order one afternoon and was struck by the physical fact of them.

“Good God,” he said.

His wife, who was darning at the window, looked up.

“Has it become bad?”

“It has become extensive.”

“That was always the danger.”

“It may be unreadable.”

“Yes,” she said. “But now it is unreadable in earnest.”

He laughed, though not without unease.

There are points in any labor at which one no longer wants encouragement so much as witness. To be told a thing is admirable is of less use than to have someone concede that it exists.

On a Sunday evening, walking after supper by the lane beyond the churchyard, they found the hedges fully green in the loose, new manner of leaves not yet thickened to summer conviction. The fields had that impossible color which seems painted from memory rather than observed. A boy somewhere unseen was practicing a whistle on one phrase and not improving it. Farther off a dog barked with intermittent relevance.

“Do you ever think,” he said, “how much of life is made of recurring things we insist on receiving as if for the first time?”

“Only the good recurring things,” she said. “Nobody greets a bill with wonder.”

“The apple blossom.”

“Yes.”

“The first swallows.”

“Yes.”

“The smell after rain.”

She nodded.

“That is because repetition is not sameness. It is renewal, which is a very different arrangement.”

He turned this over.

“You make it sound theological.”

“No. Merely practical. If things returned exactly as they were, nobody could bear it.”

They walked on. A little wind moved through the ash above them with the thin new sound leaves have before the year gives them weight. In the churchyard the stones looked less solemn for being half overtaken by grass. Everything alive appeared engaged in some effort that was neither dramatic nor optional.

Back at the house the windows showed light in the lower rooms, soft behind the panes. As they came through the gate, Finch herself crossed the path before them, no longer merely mother but already regaining the independent air with which cats decline to be wholly defined by service. One kitten, escaped or promoted, sat on the step and contemplated the world with an expression of private criticism.

“There,” said his wife. “The age of innocence is over.”

“It lasted nearly three weeks.”

“Longer than in some species.”

Inside, the lamp was lit though evening had not quite finished. Mrs. Finch had left dough covered to rise and gone home, taking with her the day’s account of grievances. A pan on the range made small competent sounds. On the table lay his sister’s letter, the seed catalog, a spoon somebody had no excuse for leaving there, and three pages of manuscript he had brought down to revise and had not touched. Such mild confusions, accumulating daily and corrected in part, gave the room its peculiar honesty. A perfectly ordered house may be admirable, but an inhabited one offers better evidence.

He stood a moment without moving further in.

“What is it?” his wife asked.

“Nothing,” he said. Then, because it was not nothing: “Only that one is sometimes overtaken by the fact of having a life.”

She looked at him with that mixture of amusement and kindness which keeps solemnity from hardening into nonsense.

“Well,” she said, “do not just stand in the passage having it. Shut the door. You are letting in the evening.”

And because this was also true, he did.
