May entered not with trumpets but by the window, which was found one morning to admit, along with the light, a smell of hawthorn from somewhere beyond immediate ownership. This was the sort of thing the year did when it wished to be forgiven for April. Even Mrs. Finch, whose standards in such matters were exacting and whose confidence in seasonal reform remained slight, conceded that the air had “improved its manners.”

The improvement was not universal. The weeds, encouraged by rain, warmth, and inattention wherever these could be found together, came up with a democratic vigor that made no distinction between path, bed, and respectable gravel. He spent an hour stooping among the onions and rose with a handful of green offenders, a painful back, and no conviction that the garden had noticed.

“It notices,” said his wife. “It merely refuses gratitude.”

“That seems ungenerous.”

“Yes. Nature is very free with beauty and extremely close with thanks.”

The kittens, having progressed from helplessness to intention, now regarded the house as a series of problems improperly solved by human beings. The black one had learned to descend from chairs by pretending not to mind the drop. The white one preserved its clerical gravity but applied it to increasingly secular investigations, including the cream jug. The patched one no longer required betrayal by success; it launched itself at curtains, skirts, trouser legs, and once the lower shelf of the bookcase with a confidence that implied architecture existed principally for its rehearsal. The mottled one, the politician, had begun to purr in advance of being picked up, as if to suggest that affection, properly managed, ought never to be left until after the event.

“They are becoming persons,” he said, watching them patrol the rug with uncertain tails.

“No,” said his wife. “Persons become them. It happens much earlier.”

His manuscript entered a stage less like composition than excavation. Passages he had admired looked suddenly as though written by a man with excellent intentions and very little ear. Others, which he scarcely remembered setting down, held their place with a composure he resented. To revise is to discover how much of one’s confidence was based upon not looking closely. He crossed out three pages before breakfast and restored two of them after tea, which gave the day an air of activity without quite proving progress.

At luncheon Mrs. Finch observed him regarding his plate in abstraction and said, “If you are planning to improve something, sir, I hope it is not the pudding. It has settled as far as Christian humility requires.”

“I was thinking about a chapter.”

“Then think after eating. Empty people produce windy work.”

His wife lowered her eyes in that way she had when choosing between reproof and enjoyment.

“She is not wrong,” she said.

“It is oppressive,” he replied, “to be outnumbered by practicality.”

“Yes,” said Mrs. Finch. “That is why it exists.”

From the village came reports of advancement and alarm in nearly equal measure. Mrs. Beddow’s pears continued to justify a tone of personal merit. The rector’s wife had put in annuals “for color,” provoking from Mrs. Finch the dark remark that color without structure was simply noise in petal form. Young Mr. Hale lost six cabbages in one night to something nobody had seen and everybody identified. There was discussion at the post office of slugs, though conducted with the gravity of border policy.

The rector himself called one damp afternoon with a book he thought might interest him and stayed to be shown the kittens, who received theology with tolerance. The white one climbed, by stages both hesitant and inevitable, into the cave of his sleeve and fell asleep there.

“I begin,” said the rector, scarcely moving, “to understand certain medieval legends better than I did.”

“About saints?”

“About creatures choosing them. It is a much more embarrassing form of election.”

His wife, threading wool through the eye of a needle with narrowed attention, said, “Most elections are.”

The apple blossom did not last, as no one had expected it to, but in falling it managed a final extravagance, laying the grass under the tree with an appearance of celebration after the guests had gone. He came upon it in the slant light of evening and thought, not for the first time, that there are forms of waste which seem richer than economy. By morning the petals had browned at the edges and were trodden into the path by feet insufficiently poetic, which did not lessen the truth of the thing.

His sister wrote again. This letter was shorter, which he mistrusted more. She was better, she said, except on those days when she was not; the weather disagreed with her and so did most arrangements made by others. Their cousin in Bath had undertaken a cure. The maid remained impossible. Would he advise? He carried the letter in his pocket until he had formed three replies and believed in none of them.

“What do you want to say?” asked his wife.

“That she magnifies every discomfort until it casts a shadow over the furniture.”

“No. What do you want to say kindly?”

He considered.

“That I am sorry she is low. That I know it feels real. That I cannot conduct her life for her by post.”

“There,” said his wife. “Now remove the third sentence and soften the second.”

“I shall be left with very little.”

“Sympathy often is. That is why people value it.”

He wrote at the dining table while the last of the light held. The mottled kitten slept on his foot, reducing the circulation but lending, he felt, a moral pressure against impatience. When he had finished, the letter seemed neither wise nor useful, but it was at least human, which is often the nearest practical substitute.

The beans came up. This event, prepared for by so much planning and foretold with so much caution, occurred in silence and looked at first unimpressive, as important developments often do. Mrs. Finch inspected the rows with guarded approval.

“Well,” she said, “they have chosen to attend.”

“You speak of them as if they were guests.”

“So they are. Guests with habits. If neglected, they sulk. If overindulged, they run to leaf. If discussed in front of them, they disappoint one on purpose.”

He had by then lived long enough among gardeners to know that plants are rarely permitted to remain botanical. They become moral examples, local scandals, proofs of intelligence, or objects of grievance according to their behavior under observation.

One afternoon of bright wind and moving cloud he took his pages outdoors, settled in the chair by the south wall, and accomplished almost nothing except keeping them from blowing into the thyme. Yet the unproductive hour left him less oppressed than a diligent morning indoors. Above him, swallows stitched and corrected the air with reckless exactness. Nearby, his wife tied up sweet peas with lengths of soft twine that made her look, from where he sat, as though she were performing some very patient kind of blessing.

“Have you written?” she asked.

“Not usefully.”

“But have you sat there with intention?”

“Yes.”

“Then the day is not wholly lost. Intention also requires exercise.”

“That sounds suspiciously like encouragement.”

“It is much cheaper.”

Toward evening a shower passed over so briefly that the west remained gold while the drops still struck the flagstones. The smell that rose afterward from the ground seemed larger than the garden, as if the earth beyond the hedges had joined in. The kittens, forbidden the wet for reasons they considered tyrannical, lined themselves along the threshold and watched the rain with the collective resentment of a committee denied jurisdiction.

The patched one escaped first, as was natural. It returned darkened, startled, and inflated with grievance, having discovered that weather could touch back.

“There,” said his wife, rubbing it dry in a square of old linen. “Experience.”

“It does not appear improved by it.”

“No. But it has enlarged its field of complaint.”

Later, when the lamps were lit and the house had drawn in upon its own circle of brightness, he found himself again arrested by the ordinary spectacle of things continuing: the clock pursuing its patient theft; the pan on the hob giving off a faint agreeable heat; a basket of mending waiting without reproach; the scratch of his wife’s needle; the little burred engine of a kitten purring from somewhere invisible but near. Such moments do not announce themselves as happiness. They are too furnished with spoons, drafts, half-finished tasks, and minor anxieties for that. Yet one suspects, in looking back, that happiness has often passed through on just such domestic feet.

“I was thinking,” he said.

His wife did not look up.

“This is always a dangerous introduction.”

“That people speak of peace as if it were a pause. But perhaps it is more often a continuance.”

She considered this.

“Yes,” she said. “A pause is merely an interruption with good publicity.”

He smiled.

“And continuance?”

“A privilege,” she said, biting off the thread, “which is why it resembles work.”

Outside, some late bird persisted in two notes and then silence, two notes and silence, as if trying the edges of the dark. The room held. The night, not yet warm but no longer hostile, pressed mildly at the panes. On the table beside him lay his revised chapter, his sister’s answer folded for the morning post, and a garden string catalogue nobody had put away. None of these things was complete, but all were in hand, which for many purposes amounts to the same kind of hope.

If you like, I can continue this into June in the same voice.

turns.speaker: A
turns.content_clean:
June arrived as if it had been consulting maps unavailable to the rest of the year and had chosen, with some care, the exact moment at which the hedges should look self-satisfied. Everything broadened. The leaves, which in May had still possessed something of youth’s translucence, now settled into competence. The roses opened with that air of having meant it all along. Even the weeds, no longer merely opportunistic, took on the confidence of an occupying force.

Mrs. Finch regarded the borders one morning with her hands beneath her apron and said, “Now it begins.”

“What begins?”

“The season in earnest. Spring is promise. This is administration.”

He thought this severe, but the garden supported her. It had ceased to be a matter of surprises and become instead a system of demands, all pressing their claims at once. There was tying to be done, watering to be judged, deadheading to be anticipated, thinning postponed beyond reason and then performed in remorse. The beans, having “chosen to attend,” as Mrs. Finch had put it, now appeared determined to dominate the conversation.

His wife went out after breakfast with a basket on her arm and returned with strawberries enough to give pleasure and not enough to permit greed.

“The first are always a moral quantity,” she said. “They remind one that delight must begin by being shared.”

“That is a remarkably convenient principle when there are only seven.”

“Nine.”

“One of them was malformed.”

“Then it had character.”

The kittens, promoted by growth into fresh disobediences, had entered that stage at which innocence is no longer plausible but remains, by force of charm, legally useful. The black one had developed speed without judgment. The white one maintained its appearance of ecclesiastical reserve while acquiring a taste for ambush. The patched one treated every ascent as justified by the view from halfway. The mottled one had discovered that if it sat very still in the passage and looked ornamental, someone would eventually commit the error of trusting it.

There are in every house certain negotiations which never conclude but only pass, from day to day, into new examples. Whether cats may be on tables was one. Whether manuscripts are safer inside drawers or under paperweights was another. Whether a basket of clean laundry ought to be regarded as furniture, weather, or challenge had become, through repeated experiment, a subject on which the kittens held advanced opinions.

He found the white one asleep on his pages and said so in a tone meant to invite allied indignation.

His wife looked over.

“Well,” she said, “it is seeking culture in the warmest available form.”

“It is creasing Chapter Eleven.”

“Then Chapter Eleven should emerge humbler.”

At the village, June produced its annual confusion of fecundity and complaint. The rector’s wife’s annuals had exceeded expectation in precisely the manner that invited criticism. Mrs. Finch, returning from some errand under protest, reported that they were “making a scene.”

“In what colors?” asked his wife.

“All of them,” said Mrs. Finch darkly. “And none with breeding.”

Young Mr. Hale’s cabbages continued to suffer depredations from agencies no one had seen and everyone described with technical certainty. Mrs. Beddow, whose pears now required no prompting to become a topic, had begun saying “of course” before observations which no one had contested. At the post office there was strong feeling about blackfly, conveyed by persons whose tone suggested foreign powers.

He worked, if that was the word, through the month with a diligence that altered little from the outside but felt laborious within. Summer exposes weak sentences. In winter one may smuggle a good deal under the confidence of firelight and weather; in June everything asks to be read plainly. He took to carrying pages into the garden, where they acquired an authority from being clipped beneath a flowerpot and a vulnerability from bees.

One afternoon he read aloud a passage to his wife, who was shelling peas with the grave efficiency of one conducting a green inquiry.

“Well?” he said when he had finished.

“It improves.”

“That is not approval.”

“No. It is hope in workmanlike dress.”

“I had aimed at something more distinct.”

“Yes,” she said, letting peas fall softly into the bowl. “But if one waited for distinction before continuing, most things would remain chairs in timber.”

Her capacity for reducing loftier anxieties to household scale should perhaps have offended him more than it did. In fact it often spared him. There are few vanities that survive long when measured against laundry, vegetables, correspondence, and the question of whether the rain-barrel has properly filled.

His sister wrote again, at greater length and with improved penmanship, which he mistrusted even more than brevity. There had been, she said, one tolerable day followed by two impossible ones. The cousin in Bath persisted in optimism. A new tonic had been recommended by a person of standing. The maid had left, or threatened to, which in practical terms amounted to the same atmosphere. She hoped he was not overworking.

He read this in the sitting room and made a sound which caused the mottled kitten, asleep on the windowsill, to open one eye in administrative concern.

“What now?” asked his wife.

“She inquires after my health in the same letter in which she dismantles her own.”

“Yes,” said his wife. “Ill people often become territorial.”

“That is not charitable.”

“No. But it may still be useful.”

He sat with the letter on his knee.

“I do not know whether to answer her spirits or her statements.”

“Spirits first,” said his wife. “Statements are much less lonely, but they make more noise.”

So he wrote again; and because June had enlarged everything, the act seemed less dutiful than before, part of the same general business by which one tied, watered, thinned, and endured. A life, he was beginning to see, is maintained by many forms of staking.

There came a spell of heat so sudden that the house itself appeared to draw a slower breath. Doors stood open. Flies conducted themselves with irritating assurance. The table by the window became headquarters for cool drinks, unanswered notes, seed packets not yet discarded, and the kind of books one means to dip into and instead leaves face-down in surrender. Mrs. Finch declared that pastry was now a risk rather than a contribution and shifted her loyalties to cold syllabubs.

“The weather,” she said, “is becoming self-important.”

The roses answered it magnificently. For three or four days the garden enjoyed its own perfection in a manner that was almost bad for it. Visitors slowed at the gate. Passersby found reasons to pause. Even he felt, during those temporary evenings when the light seemed less to fade than to reconsider, that some apology might be owed to existence for the frequency with which he had judged it hurriedly.

The apology was not requested. Greenfly arrived. One of the delphiniums leaned in a manner too eloquent to ignore. The patched kitten climbed into the herb bed and emerged perfumed but unrepentant. A plate left with cream at the dairy door acquired an ant-halo of biblical density. Summer, having demonstrated its generosity, resumed the more intimate liberties by which it reminds one that beauty is not the same arrangement as ease.

The rector came to supper and was induced, afterward, to walk in the garden. The white kitten accompanied him as before with a look of having accepted a chaplaincy. Near the sweet peas he paused, hands behind him, and said, “One forgets, in mid-year, how persuasive the world becomes.”

“Persuasive of what?” asked his wife.

“That continuance is enough.”

“And is it?” he said.

The rector smiled in the dimness.

“On the best evenings, almost.”

It was one of those nights in which the air remains after sunset as if reluctant to abandon a good impression. The swallows had gone low and then vanished. Somewhere beyond the hedge a child was called in and resisted according to ancient form. The roses, no longer visible in detail, made themselves known by scent instead, which is perhaps a more modest and therefore more powerful mode of society.

Later, indoors, with the windows unlatched and the curtains stirring as though in thought, he looked over the day and found it oddly difficult to divide into major and minor parts. He had revised half a chapter and spoiled one paragraph beyond immediate repair. He had posted a letter. He had eaten strawberries, tied up runner beans, rescued a saucer from the black kitten, and listened while his wife read aloud a notice from the parish sheet in which the phrase “voluntary compulsory assistance” had appeared without apparent alarm. These did not amount, separately, to consequence. Yet the day had weight.

“I think,” he said, “that I have been too ready to call things trivial when they are merely repeated.”

His wife, who was winding wool into a ball while the mottled kitten provided opposition, said, “Repetition is how life tells the truth when one is too distracted to hear it once.”

“That is annoyingly good.”

“Yes,” she said. “I save my best remarks for when your guard is down.”

Outside, the dark had not fully gathered but only deepened, as though June disliked conclusions. From the garden came the occasional soft displacement of something small among leaves, the secret, industrious life of creatures with no respect for sleep or ownership. On the table lay his pages, her mending, a bowl smelling faintly of crushed strawberries, and a coil of green string with a pair of shears set across it like a practical emblem. Nothing was finished. The month itself seemed in no haste to be. But everything, for the moment, was growing into its place as best it could, which is perhaps all ripeness ever means.

If you like, I can go on into July.

turns.speaker: A
turns.content_clean:
July entered not so much by arrival as by insistence. June had still possessed intervals of persuasion, evenings in which one might be coaxed into gratitude by scent and slanting light; but July, once established, spoke in declarations. The sun no longer argued. It occupied. Dust appeared on surfaces with the composure of precedent. The lawn, which in spring had accepted growth as its natural profession, began to consider endurance an equal distinction.

Mrs. Finch, crossing the yard with a basin and an expression of old enmity, remarked that the weather had now “settled into opinions.”

“Whose?” he asked.

“Ignorant ones,” she said. “Everything either flags or bolts, and one is expected to admire both.”

The sweet peas, however, justified themselves extravagantly. They climbed with social ambition and flowered as though each bloom had been privately promised an audience. His wife cut armfuls for the house, where they stood in jugs and bowls and whatever vessels could be persuaded into elegance, making every room smell as if it had recently received good news.

“The trouble with sweet peas,” she said, arranging them on the mantel, “is that they are too charming to be trusted.”

“How can a flower be untrustworthy?”

“It disappears while one is still thanking it.”

This seemed to him less a fault than a summary, but he did not say so because the black kitten had at that moment launched itself at a fallen tendril of vine and become entangled in a manner that combined athletic ambition with immediate regret.

The kittens, no longer very kitten-like except in self-excuse, had entered a phase of distributed criminality. The black one remained a creature of pure impulse, animated less by intention than by the discovery that motion was usually possible and often entertaining. The white one had perfected a look of remote innocence under cover of which it committed highly selective nuisances. The patched one was drawn by some inward geometry to surfaces just too narrow for prudence. The mottled one, whose mind was plainly the strongest of the four, had begun experimenting with cause and effect in relation to human habits and breakfast.

One morning his wife found the butter dishonored beyond appeal.

“This,” she said, “is no longer accident.”

The mottled kitten, seated at a careful distance and washing one paw with legal calm, declined to assist the inquiry.

“It has an investigative face,” he said.

“No,” said his wife. “It has the face of a minor official who knows the papers have already gone missing.”

The garden in July ceased pretending that any part of it could be left to character. Everything required intervention, and anything neglected at breakfast had become a principle by tea. The beans climbed. The courgettes enlarged by stealth and then all at once. Lettuce, unless gathered promptly, turned from promise to reproach. There were mornings in which he went out merely to look and returned with his arms occupied and his conscience burdened.

Mrs. Finch regarded the produce with the satisfaction of one vindicated by abundance but inconvenienced by it in practice.

“There is no moderation in vegetables,” she said. “They either fail in a mean spirit or succeed like relatives descending without notice.”

At table, peas gave way to beans, strawberries to currants, and the first raspberries appeared with that tender authority by which certain fruits abolish discussion. His wife made jam in a state of concentrated heat, while the kitchen itself seemed to participate in transformation, windows open, sleeves turned, sugar heaped with an almost ceremonial confidence. The smell rose through the house as if childhood had been boiled down to an essence and briefly made domestic again.

He stood in the doorway and was told he was in the way.

“I am observing.”

“You are casting shade where it is not wanted.”

“I had thought all shade desirable in this weather.”

“In gardens, yes. In jam, no.”

He withdrew. There are forms of usefulness best practiced as absence.

At the village, July produced a more fatigued mode of animation. Effort had ripened into commentary. The rector’s wife’s annuals continued to provoke among persons devoid of annuals the kind of moral unease ordinarily reserved for sudden wealth. Young Mr. Hale’s cabbages had now become emblematic of something larger than cabbages, though what precisely depended on the speaker and the temperature. Mrs. Beddow’s pears had swollen into such continual mention that one felt they had acquired not merely size but doctrine.

At the post office there was discussion of wasps. There is, in every summer, a point at which wasps cease to be insects and become a public atmosphere. Persons who in winter would have disagreed on theology exchanged practical convictions regarding jam cupboards, fallen fruit, and the proper use of saucers. One heard of nests in tones formerly employed for scandals.

He worked through the heat as one rows through water that appears calm and resists by totality. Morning offered some hope. By noon the pages seemed to give off a faint repellent brightness, as if the unrevised had discovered climate as an ally. Ink dried too quickly. Thought dried more quickly still. He found himself composing sentences whose chief merit was that they were less bad than the previous ones, and this species of progress, though authentic, lacked glamour.

His wife, encountering him one afternoon in a condition of literary hostility, asked whether the chapter was recalcitrant.

“It is neither alive nor dead,” he said. “It merely persists.”

“Then it resembles a good many respectable things.”

“I cannot tell whether it wants cutting or courage.”

“Usually both,” she said.

She was stoning cherries with a concentration that made philosophy look idle.

“It has become flat,” he said.

“Perhaps you have looked at it too long from the same chair.”

This irritated him because it was plausible. He took the pages outdoors, where the bees, moving among lavender with a seriousness beyond vanity, seemed to rebuke fuss while justifying labor. The delphinium that had leaned in June now required outright rescue and was secured to its stake with green string in the posture of a person helped through indiscretion. Nearby the roses, less imperial than before but still persuasive, had begun to drop petals in soft evidence that magnificence also sheds.

His sister wrote once more. The letter was shorter, which made it worse. Brevity, in her case, had the quality of curtains drawn during daylight. There had been a setback, though whether in health, temper, servants, or conviction was not at first plain. The cousin in Bath remained “steadfast,” a word that conveyed both gratitude and fatigue. There was mention of expense. There was no mention of sleep.

He read this by the open window while flies attempted intimacy with the pane.

“Well?” said his wife.

“I cannot decide whether she wishes comfort, advice, or witness.”

“Yes,” said his wife. “People rarely sort their needs before posting them.”

“She says very little.”

“She says enough to be answered.”

He turned the page over and back again.

“I never know whether my letters help.”

“Most help is less dramatic than the asker hoped and more necessary than the giver feels.”

So he wrote, not well at first, then better by forgetting to compose. The afternoon was hot, the room untidy, the patched cat asleep in the work-basket as if storage had been invented for its personal convenience. Outside, someone passed the gate pushing a bicycle and singing incompletely. The ordinary persisted around the act of concern, not insulting it but containing it; and perhaps there was mercy in that.

Toward the middle of the month came thunder, long threatened and theatrically withheld. The day had been close from breakfast onward, the air thick not merely with heat but with suspense. Leaves showed their paler undersides. Swallows flew low with the urgent economy of creatures who have read the matter correctly. Even Mrs. Finch, not generally susceptible to atmosphere, said that the weather was “waiting to pounce.”

It did so at last after supper. The first drops struck with individual authority; then the sky gave up negotiation entirely. Rain crossed the garden in visible force. The roses bowed, the beans rejoiced, the guttering found its voice, and the whole house listened.

His wife stood at the door and breathed in.

“There,” she said. “Now everything may stop pretending.”

He joined her. The scent rising from the soaked earth was so immediate and complete that for a moment one felt the garden had not merely been watered but translated into its own essence. Lightning showed the hedge in hard white conviction. The black cat, who had been absent on enterprises of doubtful legitimacy, came in at speed and with grievances.

Afterward the house cooled by degrees. The rain-barrel filled. The night became habitable again. In the morning all was altered, though by no rearrangement one could list quickly. Green had deepened. Dust had been abolished. The lawn, which had seemed resigned to decline, looked as if reprieve had found it deserving. Snails appeared with that post-rain confidence by which small devastations present themselves as beneficiaries.

Mrs. Finch, inspecting the herbaceous border, said only, “Well,” in a tone that included relief, criticism, and renewed employment.

The rector came a few evenings later, bringing with him a sermon not yet preached and blackcurrants not entirely volunteered by his shrubs. He sat in the garden after the sun had withdrawn from management and accepted a glass while the white cat occupied the chair beside him with clerical decorum.

“There is something curious about July,” he said. “It is both culmination and warning.”

“Warning of what?” asked his wife.

“That ripeness is already half memory.”

She considered this.

“That is very rectorial.”

“It is. I have been practicing.”

They walked later among the borders, which in that hour between heat and dark contrived to look both lavish and tired, like a hostess after excellent company. The phlox had begun. The lilies performed themselves with a confidence so complete it bordered on indecency. Moths moved where bees had been, gentler in manner and no less intent.

He said, “I think I understand summer less the older I grow.”

“That may be improvement,” said the rector. “One only thoroughly understands what has been reduced too far.”

When at last the house was shut for the night and the windows left open in cautious trust, he sat for a while over the day’s pages without advancing them. On the table lay a dish of raspberries, a letter half folded, two fallen sweet-pea petals, and a button Mrs. Finch had discovered under the settle and restored to civilization without enthusiasm. The kittens, distributed in attitudes of complete collapse, had finally worn themselves into innocence.

“What have you done today?” his wife asked, not looking up from her sewing.

He considered. He had revised three pages and doubted two of them. He had written to his sister, tied in the delphinium, fetched in the washing before the storm, and carried a pail of windfalls to the compost. He had eaten cherries. He had listened to thunder. He had rescued the black cat from the pantry and failed to determine how it had entered.

“Very little,” he said.

“Ah,” said his wife. “Then it was a full day.”

He smiled.

“That is nonsense.”

“No,” she said. “A day in which nothing dramatic happens has room enough for all the important things.”

Outside, the dark lay warm upon the garden, not empty but inhabited at every level by stirrings too small for ownership. Somewhere a late cart went by with the softened clatter that distance permits. The air through the window carried earth, leaves, and the faint sweet fatigue of flowers past their first confidence. July, for all its display, was beginning already to confess time in scents and seeds, in petals loosened, in fruit insisting on being gathered before it ceased to be itself.

Nothing was finished. The book was not finished, nor the weeding, nor the correspondence, nor the long, irregular education by which one learns to live among recurring tasks without calling them failures of imagination. But the month, in its hot and overflowering way, made incompletion seem less like deficiency than condition. Everything gave, spoiled, ripened, demanded, loosened, and began again elsewhere. Even weariness had its place in the pattern, not as defeat but as evidence of having been used by one’s life.

If you like, I can go on into August.

turns.speaker: A
turns.content_clean:
August arrived with less authority than July but more consequence. If July declared itself, August amended the terms. Its heat, when it came, was not inaugural but cumulative, as though the summer had been thinking the matter over and decided that what had already been experienced could, with sufficient application, be made more intimate. The days broadened and then, in some difficult-to-prove way, began almost at once to contract. One noticed not darkness exactly, but the first successful attempts of evening.

The garden, which in July had seemed chiefly occupied with abundance, now showed signs of preference. Some things pressed on with vulgar confidence. Others, having performed nobly, entered decline with a tact that was nearly moving. The sweet peas, still producing but less prodigally, had acquired that touching air of beauty continued by habit after certainty has gone. The roses offered a second, less imperial conversation. The lavender held its color like a principle. Bees persisted among it with the stern absorption of persons unwilling to discuss the calendar.

His wife, cutting back what had become too expansive for innocence, said, “August is the month in which one discovers what was bluffing.”

“What, in the garden?”

“In everything. Plants, promises, and plans for self-improvement.”

Mrs. Finch, who was gathering beans with punitive efficiency, gave a short sound indicating agreement too obvious to merit speech.

The beans had now ceased to climb and began instead to arrive. There is a stage in every productive kitchen garden when vegetables are no longer an offering but an argument. Courgettes appeared under leaves in dimensions suggesting private resentment. Marrows emerged from concealment with the gross triumph of vulgar facts. Tomatoes, after weeks of moral uncertainty, at last committed themselves to redness all at once, as if anxious to make up in simultaneity what they had lacked in punctuality.

“We ought to have picked these yesterday,” he said, looking at a collection of beans whose youth had become historical.

“We ought,” said his wife, “to have been several more efficient people for at least a fortnight.”

The blackberries along the lane began to darken, not evenly but by insinuation. Children were reported in hedgerows with tins. Fingers appeared at gates stained purple beyond argument. There was renewed village controversy over rights of picking, with much invocation of custom by persons whose chief allegiance was to whichever custom favored them that week. Mrs. Beddow maintained that blackberries from the lower lane had “a medicinal afterthought,” though whether this was praise or warning depended on whether she had been crossed.

At table, the season thickened. Plums entered, carrying in with them that peculiar mixture of luxury and slight alarm proper to fruits that bruise while being admired. There were more tomatoes than menus. Cucumbers accumulated with a politeness no one believed in. His wife, whose powers of preservation now stood in a relation to the pantry not unlike military command, put up chutney, bottled fruit, and discussed jars with a severity from which he discreetly retired.

He had once asked why preserving induced in sensible people a manner so nearly strategic.

“Because,” she had replied, “summer is generous in exactly the form most difficult to keep.”

In August the wasps prospered into insolence. No longer merely present, they advanced claims. Jam became contested territory. Teacups required vigilance. Fallen pears enacted diplomacy with decay while wasps attended them in numbers suggesting jurisdiction. Even the rector, habitually inclined toward charitable interpretation, was heard to say that the creatures possessed “an almost doctrinal objection to peace.”

The kittens, now cats except when seeking exemption, altered with the month. Youth ceased to excuse them, though not in their own estimate. The mottled one had developed a practical understanding of open windows and human inattention. The white one, having cultivated elegance, discovered that elegance increased the likelihood of forgiveness and embraced the fact as social philosophy. The patched cat retained its devotion to improbable resting places and was found one afternoon asleep in the fruit bowl with an expression implying that the arrangement, though modest, had possibilities. The black cat ranged further afield and returned from expeditions carrying burrs, rumor, and once a pheasant feather so nearly its own length that it looked for an instant like an idea too large for implementation.

His work did not improve so much as continue under less obvious protest. There were mornings in which he believed the chapter might at last be persuaded into sense, and afternoons in which sense itself seemed a provincial standard unsuited to ambition. August did not sharpen thought, but it altered its pace. The pressure to achieve gave way, on better days, to the slower duty of remaining with what had not yet yielded. He cut. He crossed out. He restored what he had cut and then cut it differently.

His wife, glancing over pages laid out to discompose him, said, “You have reached the stage of improvement invisible to visitors.”

“Then perhaps it is imaginary.”

“Not at all. The most necessary changes usually are.”

He looked at the manuscript with the tired dislike one reserves for things intimately known and imperfectly loved.

“I begin to suspect the book would prefer another author.”

“Many worthwhile things do,” she said. “One must persist in disappointing them.”

His sister wrote again, this time at greater length but with less force, as though fatigue had become not episode but climate. There had been some rallying, followed by no dependable continuation of it. The cousin in Bath, though still steadfast, was said to be “not young enough for optimism in bulk.” There were references to sleep now, which was perhaps either hope or surrender; in illness and trouble these often borrow one another’s clothes. He answered more promptly than before. Repetition had worn away the wish to say something definitive and left in its place the more serviceable intention to say something true.

Outside his window, August moved in layers of sound. Bees in the sedums. A cart beyond the hedge. The occasional dropping thud of overripe fruit. Once, during the composition of a sentence whose difficulties seemed chiefly moral, he heard his wife laughing in the yard with Mrs. Finch over a basket of tomatoes split beyond redemption, and the laughter, though he could not have said why, made it easier to proceed.

Later came the first morning unmistakably altered by season. It was not cold, but the air at breakfast carried a coolness that had crossed a threshold and would not be argued back. The sunlight remained generous, yet something in it had changed from occupation to illumination. Dust motes no longer looked triumphant, merely revealed. Even the leaves on the pear tree had acquired edges.

“August has remembered September,” his wife said.

Mrs. Finch, who mistrusted poetry unless accidental, said, “Nights are drawing in,” and considered the matter fully handled.

Harvest moved at the edges of everything. Fields beyond the village altered color in stages one could miss only by never looking. There was a week of tractors and comment, of weather watched not as topic but adjudicator. Men stood at gates with forearms on the top bar and considered clouds in silence weighted by practical theology. The rector, encountering him on the lane, said that sermons on providence were always easier before harvest began and harder after one had looked at the sky for six consecutive days.

The church fete occurred under a sun too warm for wool and too bright for scruple. Tables appeared on the lawn with the temporary confidence of summer institutions. There were sponge cakes of aggressive virtue, marrows offered in a spirit halfway between pride and surrender, painted jars, books no one would read again, and a competition involving jam whose moral seriousness exceeded its stated purpose. Children moved in shrill diagonals. Elderly ladies sat under hats broad enough to suggest municipal authority. The white cat, having followed uninvited and behaved as if on a diocesan errand, was removed by his wife before it could be entered in any category.

At the produce stall, Mrs. Finch sold beans with an expression that implied she was parting with them only because civilization had made some concessions unavoidable.

“They’re too old for best,” she told one customer, “but so are most of us, and we do for stewing.”

The customer, being wise, bought two pounds.

By late month the hedges had begun to look burdened rather than flourishing. Seedheads stood where bloom had been, not sadly but with a changed office. The lilies were mostly memories in stalk-form. Phlox thickened the evening air. Michaelmas daisies, still only in preparation, hinted from the margins at stronger colors to come. One afternoon he found his wife quiet in the border, secateurs in one hand, a trug at her feet.

“What are you doing?”

“Encouraging reality.”

She lifted the cut stems.

“If one deadheads in time, things may go on a little. If one does not, they become historical at once.”

He looked over the garden: the gone-over roses, the beans with blackened leaves at their bases, the sunflowers entering coarseness, the last sweet peas still improbably exquisite.

“It all seems more itself now,” he said.

“Yes,” she answered. “Because it has stopped trying to be only beautiful.”

At night there were moments already touched with autumn’s rehearsal. A smell of damp from places that had been dry for weeks. An owl once, from somewhere beyond the orchard. Moths striking the lamp with soft, erroneous confidence. The house, though still open to air, began on certain evenings to collect its own warmth again. The cats discovered rugs with renewed conviction. Somewhere in a drawer, though not yet consulted, lay the memory of thicker clothes.

One Sunday the rector dined with them and brought, instead of blackcurrants, a distracted manner and a basket of apples too early to be trusted.

“They fell,” he said defensively.

“Many things do,” said his wife. “That is not the same as being ready.”

The apples proved sharp enough to improve conversation. After supper they sat outside while there was still light enough to flatter everything. Bats appeared with that abruptness by which evening amends itself. The rector, looking across the garden where the last sun had found the hollyhocks and made relics of them, said, “August is kinder than July, but less forgiving.”

“In what way?”

“It shows the cost of delay.”

His wife considered this.

“That may be true in sermons and runner beans,” she said. “Not necessarily elsewhere.”

He thought of his manuscript, his unanswered letters from months before, his sister’s contained unhappiness, the delphinium that had not recovered as fully as he had claimed.

“Perhaps elsewhere too,” he said.

When at last the month began unmistakably to slope toward ending, there came a run of clear days with cool mornings and afternoons so bright they seemed less warm than golden by decision. Spiders prospered. Webs declared themselves on hedges and gate-latches, impossible to account for because they had plainly not all been spun since dawn and yet had certainly not existed the evening before. Pears dropped in the night. The grass, relieved by earlier rain and no longer bullied by heat, attempted a modest return. He found, to his surprise, that he wanted to work.

Not heroically. Not with those violent hopes by which one ruins both sentence and afternoon. But steadily. The book, reduced by revision and trouble to something nearer its actual shape, no longer repelled him quite so actively. He sat in the open window and wrote three pages that did not shame the previous two. It would have been too much to call this triumph. It was, however, relationship.

His wife, hearing this report, nodded as if informed that the beans had resumed after rain.

“There,” she said. “That is how things usually mend.”

“How?”

“Without drama. By continuing.”

That evening they ate tomatoes with bread and salt, then plums, and afterward walked to the gate for no reason except that the air invited it. The lane lay in a stillness not empty but listening. Somewhere far off a dog barked at nothing anyone could improve. The hedges smelled of dust, leaves, and the faint wine-like sweetness of things beyond their first innocence. Above them the sky retained light in long layers, each paler than the one below, as though day were withdrawing by courtesy.

“Summer is changing,” he said.

“It always was,” said his wife.

He looked back at the house: windows open, one lamp lit, the shape of ordinary life held for the moment against encroaching dark. Inside there would be the pages on the table, a bowl of fruit, perhaps one of the cats asleep where it should not be, and the small untidy continuities by which a household proves itself alive. Beyond lay other months, with their economies and relinquishments. But August, standing where fullness first admits finitude, seemed less a conclusion than an education in measure. Not the denial of plenty, but its interpretation. Fruit must be picked. Beans must be finished with. Seeds must be saved or ignored. Letters must be answered while answer is still possible. One cannot keep the whole garden flowering. One can only go out each day and participate in what is ripening, fading, asking, or ready.

If you like, September has its own intelligence.
